advisor.summary: For mixed business-personal trips, the deductible outcome is decided mostly before the trip is taken. Domestic transportation is all-or-nothing on the trip's primary purpose under Reg. §1.162-2(b) — primarily business means the full airfare deducts even with personal days attached; primarily personal means none of it, even if real work happened. Lodging and meals follow the day count either way, and the counting rules are generous to planners: travel days count, client-required standby days count, and a weekend sandwiched between business days counts when going home is impractical. Foreign trips carry a harder allocation regime under §274(c) with two safe harbors worth designing into the itinerary, and spouse costs are nondeductible without employee status and a bona fide role. Advisory: the value is trip design and a contemporaneous file, not a number the engine can honestly compute.
mechanics: Reg. §1.162-2(b) makes domestic transportation all-or-nothing on primary purpose, with time devoted to each activity the most important factor — win the day count and the round-trip fare deducts in full; lose it and the fare is entirely personal.
On-site costs allocate by day regardless of the transportation answer: lodging, meals at 50 percent under §274(n), and local costs deduct for business days only.

Business days include travel days, days the client requires presence even if little work occurs, and intervening weekends or holidays when returning home is impractical — a Friday-and-Monday meeting schedule makes the weekend count for lodging and meals.

Foreign travel allocates transportation between business and personal days under §274(c) unless the trip runs one week or less or personal time stays under 25 percent — safe harbors to schedule into, not discover afterward.

Spouse and companion costs are nondeductible under §274(m)(3) unless the spouse is a bona fide employee traveling for a genuine business purpose — and even then the lodging deduction is the single-room rate, not half the double.

§274(d) makes travel a strict-substantiation category: amount, dates, destination, and business purpose, recorded contemporaneously — the practical standard is a per-trip file of itinerary, meeting confirmations, and receipts built during the trip.

requirements: A genuine business reason for the destination, documented before departure.
A day-by-day itinerary distinguishing business from personal days, retained with calendar entries and confirmations.
Receipts for transportation and lodging assembled during the trip, not at filing time.
For spouse costs: employee status and a real business role, or exclusion of those costs.
risks: The leading audit theory is the vacation with a meeting attached: a trip that is really personal fails the primary-purpose test, zeroing the transportation deduction — and under the Sanford strict-substantiation line, reconstructed records leave no estimate to fall back on.
Foreign trips outside the safe harbors require an allocation many preparers never make — an automatic adjustment when examined.
Spouse airfare and the double-room premium deducted without employee status is a recurring, easily spotted adjustment.
Aggressive day counts — an hour of email does not make a business day — invite recharacterization of the whole trip.
stateNotes: Conformity: travel deductions ride inside federal business income, and conformity states absorb them without separate computation.
PTET interaction: entity-paid travel reduces the pass-through entity tax base like any ordinary deduction; no separate PTET step exists for this strategy.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting points (RSMo §143.121, §143.431) with no travel-specific modification.

client.teaser: A few scheduling habits turn more of each trip into a deduction.
client.headline: Plan trips so the business part actually gets deducted
plainEnglish: When a trip mixes business and pleasure, the tax result depends on how the trip is built. Here is the surprising rule for U.S. trips: if the trip is mainly business, the entire airfare is deductible — even with beach days attached. If it is mainly personal, none of the airfare counts.

Hotels and meals follow the days themselves. Business days count; personal days do not. And the calendar is a tool: meetings on Friday and Monday can make the weekend between them count. Keeping an overseas trip inside certain time limits protects the whole fare.

The other half is a simple habit. Keep a small trip file — itinerary, meeting confirmations, receipts — as you go. It takes minutes, and it is the difference between deductions that survive questions and deductions that vanish.
client.analogy: Two travelers can take the same trip and spend the same money — and only the one who planned the calendar gets the deduction.
